summary: Specifies EAP-IKEv2, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method based on IKEv2. It gives mutual authentication and session key setup, supporting passwords, shared keys and public key certificates. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: This reuses the handshake from a VPN protocol as a way to log into a network. Both sides prove who they are and agree on secret keys.

questions: how to derive keys in eap-ikev2
subtitle: Mutual authentication and session key setup using the VPN handshake protocol.

tldr.problem: Networks need secure ways for a client and server to prove who they are and establish shared encryption keys. Different scenarios require different credential types: passwords, shared keys, or certificates.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-IKEv2 reuses the handshake from IKEv2 (a VPN protocol) as an authentication method. Both sides prove their identity and negotiate cryptographic algorithms in four encrypted messages, then derive session keys.
tldr.outcome: The protocol provides mutual authentication, strong encryption, and defends against certain attacks. However, it remains experimental and has not been widely deployed.

today: RFC 5106 defines an experimental authentication method that combines the benefits of IKEv2 with the EAP framework. It remains experimental and has not been adopted as a standard; it is not widely deployed in production networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
EAP-IKEv2 is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method based on the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2). It provides mutual authentication and session key establishment between an EAP peer (a device seeking access) and an EAP server (the access control system). The protocol supports three main types of authentication credentials: asymmetric key pairs (certificates), passwords, and high-entropy shared keys. Each side can use a different credential type; for example, the server might authenticate with a certificate while the peer uses a password.

The design is split into four use cases: both sides use certificates; server uses certificate and peer uses a symmetric key; server uses certificate and peer uses a password; or both use symmetric keys. The RFC emphasizes that deriving a symmetric key from a password is insecure in some modes due to dictionary attacks.
sections.eli5: A school wants to let students in, but only if they prove they go to the school. Different students carry different IDs: some have a photo card, some have a secret password, and some have a special key. This protocol lets the school check any of these and give the student a hall pass.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
EAP-IKEv2 involves a two-roundtrip exchange followed by either success or failure. The server always initiates; the peer responds. Messages 1 and 2 are a standard EAP Identity exchange. Message 3 starts the actual EAP-IKEv2 protocol: the server sends a Security Association (SA) payload listing the cryptographic algorithms it will accept, a Diffie-Hellman value (KEi), and a nonce. The peer selects an algorithm, generates its own Diffie-Hellman value (KEr) and nonce, then computes shared keying material called SKEYSEED and derives per-direction encryption and integrity keys.

Message 4 contains the peer's choice of algorithm and its Diffie-Hellman contribution. In some modes, it also carries the peer's identity encrypted with keys derived from the shared secret. Message 5 is an encrypted payload containing the server's identity and authentication proof (a signature or MAC). Message 6 is the peer's encrypted response with its identity and authentication proof. If both sides verify successfully, the server sends EAP-Success and both sides derive a Master Session Key (MSK) and Extended Master Session Key (EMSK).
sections.eli5: The server says, "I accept these kinds of IDs, and here is my secret number." The peer answers, "I pick this kind of ID, here is my secret number too, and my ID is secret (locked up)." The server unlocks it, proves who it is, and the peer proves who it is back. Then they both shake hands and get a magic key that works from now on.

sections.title: Fast Reconnect
sections.content:
EAP-IKEv2 defines an optional fast reconnect mode for efficient re-authentication after an initial full authentication. When the server sends its authentication message, it includes a Next Fast-ID (NFID) payload containing a pseudonym identity the peer can use in future reconnect attempts. This pseudonym is opaque to the peer but allows the server to quickly map it back to the original security context without repeating the full authentication.

On reconnection, the peer sends the fast-reconnect identity in the EAP Identity Response. If the server recognizes it, it sends a CREATE_CHILD_SA request (borrowing terminology from IKEv2) with optional fresh Diffie-Hellman values. The peer responds with matching values. This shortens the exchange from six messages to five, and the keys are derived differently: new keying material comes from the old SK_d value mixed with fresh nonces and optionally new Diffie-Hellman material.
sections.eli5: After the first time, the server gives the student a special fast-pass card with a secret number on it. Next time the student comes back, they show the fast-pass card and say, "I am the student who did the full check-in before." The server checks the card and lets them in without doing all the checks again.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Session Keys
sections.content:
Once EAP-IKEv2 completes successfully, both sides generate session keys for use elsewhere. The protocol generates 128 octets of keying material by applying a pseudorandom function to the agreed-upon SK_d key with the two nonces as input. The first 64 octets become the Master Session Key (MSK) for use by other protocols (such as WPA2 in wireless networks), and the second 64 octets become the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) for auxiliary services.

The protocol also exports three information elements for key management: a Session-ID (constructed from the EAP type and both nonces), a Peer-ID (from the peer's identification payload), and a Server-ID (from the server's identification payload). These identifiers help the key management framework track and manage the keys across the network.
sections.eli5: After the handshake, the two sides use a magical recipe to mix their secret numbers and make 128 magic tokens. Half the tokens are for the student to use, half are for the school to use. They also each remember where the agreement came from, who did it, and when.

sections.title: Security Properties
sections.content:
EAP-IKEv2 claims to provide mutual authentication (both sides prove their identity), integrity protection of the protocol exchange, replay protection (nonces make each run unique), confidentiality of certain fields, ciphersuite negotiation that is protected once keys are established, and session independence such that learning old keys does not compromise new sessions. The protocol supports perfect forward secrecy if Diffie-Hellman values are discarded after each exchange.

In scenarios where the peer authenticates with a password, the protocol requires the server to authenticate first (as the initiator), which prevents offline dictionary attacks on the password. However, the RFC warns that symmetric keys MUST NOT be derived from passwords in certain modes, and that online dictionary attacks are still possible unless the server implements rate limiting on failed attempts.
sections.eli5: The handshake makes sure both sides are real (not phonies), the messages do not get changed, and no one can replay old messages. If someone steals an old secret, it does not help them with new ones. If a student uses a password, the server proves it is the real server first, which stops guessing attacks.

sections.title: Assigned Values
sections.content: EAP-IKEv2 is assigned EAP method type 49. The protocol defines its own payload type registry separate from IKEv2, though many payload types (SA, Key Exchange, Nonce, Identification, Certificate, Authentication, Encrypted, Notification) are semantically equivalent and carry the same type values in both protocols. One unique addition is the Next Fast-ID payload (type 121), which does not exist in IKEv2. Payload types 122-127 are reserved for future EAP-IKEv2 extensions, and 128-255 are for private use.
sections.eli5: The school system assigned this way of checking IDs the number 49 so computers can recognize it. The protocol uses numbered envelopes for different kinds of information, and some of the envelope numbers match the ones used in VPN systems.
